segments.text: Begin with the big picture: matrix multiplication can be understood from several equivalent viewpoints rather than one rule to memorize.
For a small example, explain the formula entry by entry and then interpret the same output as a combination of columns.
Compare row-times-column, column combinations, and whole-matrix transformations. Ask why all three produce the same numbers.
Define an inverse through the formal equation A inverse times A equals I, after the concrete multiplication is visible.
Show a singular example and ask what goes wrong. The failed elimination step explains why not every matrix has an inverse.
Practice finding an inverse by Gauss-Jordan elimination, check the answer by multiplication, and generalize the check to a new matrix.
